{{Short description|Type of integral}}
In [[functional analysis]], '''double operator integrals''' (DOI) are integrals of the form
:<math>\operatorname{Q}_{\varphi}:=\int_{N}\int_M \varphi(x,y)\mathrm{d}E(x)\operatorname{T}\mathrm{d}F (y),</math>
where <math>\operatorname{T}:G\to H</math> is a bounded [[linear operator]] between two [[separable space|separable]] [[Hilbert space|Hilbert spaces]],
:<math>E:(N,\mathcal{A})\to P(H),</math>
:<math>F:(M,\mathcal{B})\to P(G),</math>
are two [[spectral measure]]s, where <math>P(H)</math> stands for the set of orthogonal projections over <math>H</math>, and <math>\varphi</math> is a scalar-valued [[measurable function]] called the ''symbol'' of the DOI. The integrals are to be understood in the form of [[Stieltjes integral]]s.

Double operator integrals can be used to estimate the differences of two operators and have application in [[perturbation theory]]. The theory was mainly developed by [[Mikhail Shlyomovich Birman]] and [[Mikhail Zakharovich Solomyak]] in the late 1960s and 1970s, however they appeared earlier first in a paper by Daletskii and Krein.<ref>{{cite journal|first1=Yuri. L.|last1=Daletskii|first2=Selim G.|last2=Krein|title=Integration and differentiation of functions of Hermitian operators and application to the theory of perturbations|lang=ru|journal=Trudy Sem. Po Funktsion. Analizu|volume=1 |date=1956 |pages=81–105|publisher=Voronezh State University}}</ref>

== Double operator integrals ==
The map
:<math>\operatorname{J}_{\varphi}^{E,F}:\operatorname{T}\mapsto \operatorname{Q}_{\varphi}</math>
is called a ''transformer''. We simply write <math>\operatorname{J}_{\varphi}:=\operatorname{J}_{\varphi}^{E,F}</math>, when it's clear which spectral measures we are looking at.

Originally Birman and Solomyak considered a [[Hilbert–Schmidt operator]] <math>\operatorname{T}</math> and defined a spectral measure <math>\mathcal{E}</math> by
:<math>\mathcal{E}(\Lambda\times \Delta)\operatorname{T}:=E(\Lambda)\operatorname{T}F(\Delta),\quad \operatorname{T}\in \mathcal{S}_2,</math>
for measurable sets <math>\Lambda\times \Delta\subset N \times M</math>, then the double operator integral <math>\operatorname{Q}_{\varphi}</math> can be defined as
:<math>\operatorname{Q}_{\varphi}:=\left(\int_{N\times M} \varphi(\lambda, \mu)\;\mathrm{d}\mathcal{E}(\lambda, \mu)\right)\operatorname{T}</math>
for bounded and measurable functions <math>\varphi</math>. However one can look at more general operators <math>\operatorname{T}</math> as long as <math>\operatorname{Q}_{\varphi}</math> stays bounded.

== Examples ==
=== Perturbation theory ===
Consider the case where <math>H=G</math> is a Hilbert space and let <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> be two bounded self-adjoint operators on <math>H</math>. Let <math>\operatorname{T}:=B-A</math> and <math>f</math> be a function on a set <math>S</math>, such that the spectra <math>\sigma(A)</math> and <math>\sigma(B)</math> are in <math>S</math>. As usual, <math>\operatorname{I}</math> is the identity operator. Then by the [[spectral theorem]] <math>\operatorname{J}_{\lambda}\operatorname{I}=A</math> and <math>\operatorname{J}_{\mu}\operatorname{I}=B</math> and <math>\operatorname{J}_{\mu-\lambda}\operatorname{I}=\operatorname{T}</math>, hence
:<math>f(B)-f(A)=\operatorname{J}_{f(\mu)-f(\lambda)}\operatorname{I}=\operatorname{J}_{\frac{f(\mu)-f(\lambda)}{\mu-\lambda}}\operatorname{J}_{\mu-\lambda}\operatorname{I}=\operatorname{J}_{\frac{f(\mu)-f(\lambda)}{\mu-\lambda}}\operatorname{T}=\operatorname{Q}_{\varphi}</math>
and so<ref>{{cite journal|first1=Mikhail S.|last1=Birman|first2=Mikhail Z.|last2=Solomyak|title=Double Operator Integrals in a Hilbert Space|journal=Integr. Equ. Oper. Theory|volume=47|pages=136–137|date=2003|issue=2 |doi=10.1007/s00020-003-1157-8|s2cid=122799850 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book|first1=Mikhail S.|last1=Birman|first2=Mikhail Z.|last2=Solomyak|title=Lectures on Double Operator Integrals|date=2002}}</ref>
:<math>f(B)-f(A)=\int_{\sigma(A)}\int_{\sigma(B)}\frac{f(\mu)-f(\lambda)}{\mu-\lambda}(\mu-\lambda)\mathrm{d}E_A(\lambda)\mathrm{d}F_B(\mu)=\int_{\sigma(A)}\int_{\sigma(B)}\frac{f(\mu)-f(\lambda)}{\mu-\lambda}\mathrm{d}E_A(\lambda)\operatorname{T}\mathrm{d}F_B(\mu),</math>
where <math>E_A(\cdot)</math> and <math>F_B(\cdot)</math> denote the corresponding spectral measures of <math>A</math> and <math>B</math>.
